comment: How the front of an appliance is laid out, so the plugin can draw it instead of shipping a
photograph of it. The drawing is generated as inline SVG at render time: a few kilobytes of
markup, no image files, nothing to license.
WHY NOT PHOTOGRAPHS. A vendor's product render or photograph is that vendor's copyrighted work,
and a plugin under a BSD licence cannot redistribute it. The bulk source that looks like an
answer - the NetBox device-type library - carries a CC0 label over images that are demonstrably
vendor marketing art, complete with the vendors' logos; CC0 waives only what the uploader owned
and explicitly declines to clear anyone else's rights, and that project records no provenance
for any of its 2,481 images. It also has no entry for this appliance at all.
WHAT IS SAFE. How many sockets a device has, in what order, in which bay, and what is printed
beside them are facts and short labels, and facts are not owned. So we draw from measurement,
never trace a vendor image, and never draw a logo.
THE JOIN IS DELIBERATELY WEAK. An item here names a bay and a printed label - never an interface.
The live data is matched on that pair, using chassis.json, which stays the single place where an
interface is bound to a printed name. So a wrong drawing puts a box in the wrong place; it can
never send an alert to the wrong port.
confirmed=false means nobody has stood in front of the machine and checked this layout yet. The
GUI says so, plainly, until someone confirms it with the identify button.

sophos-xg330.confirmed_note: Port order and bay grouping are corroborated by three independent witnesses on the reference machine: the owner's own interface names, the chip and PCI-subdevice boundaries, and two contiguous MAC blocks (8 addresses under one OUI for the module, 12 under another for the mainboard, in printed order). The physical ARRANGEMENT below - which row, and left-to-right position - is drawn from the owner's description and has not been checked against the metal.

rows.note: An expansion bay. Its ports enumerate before the faceplate ports, which is why PortA1 is igb0 while the printed Port1 is igb8.

These cages have no identification light this firewall can drive: the driver registers the LED node, accepts the write and nothing lights, because it drives one fixed LED index that this board does not wire. Measured on this appliance, where the copper ports do blink. Use the activity light instead - the second button on the port detail.

sophos-xgs-3300.confirmed_note: The sockets, their labels and their bays are measured: every oxp port was matched to its printed label with a cable on the appliance this project is developed on (os-xgs-npu, 2026-10-13). The left-to-right ORDER of the bays and the two-row arrangement of the copper block are drawn from the appliance's documented layout and have not yet been checked against the metal; a photograph of the front, or the owner's word, confirms it.

rows.note: Eight RJ45 in a block of two rows of four, Port1 above Port2 and so on across; the switch chip drives their LEDs from the coprocessor, so the host cannot blink them.

rows.bay: faceplate, SFP cages on the switch
rows.note: Two 1G SFP cages on the same switch chip (F3, F4). No transceiver data from the host: the cage EEPROMs are on the coprocessor's I2C.
Two 10G SFP+ cages on the coprocessor's own MAC through one 88X5113 PHY (F1, F2). Their lights are the PHY's.
The host's own gigabit NIC (igb0, printed MGMT) and the serial console; neither is a front port of the coprocessor, and the chassis table leaves igb0 with its interface name.

sophos-xgs-136.confirmed_note: The sockets, their labels and their bays are the driver's front-port table and the hardware page (os-xgs-npu, docs/hardware/xgs136.md); their left-to-right order on the panel has not been confirmed at the appliance. The rows are in label order.

rows.note: Eight RJ45 on the switch chip, labels 1 to 8; the switch drives their LEDs from the coprocessor, so the host cannot blink them.
All four on the AQR412C quad PHY on the CN9131's own ports: 9 and 10 rate-capped at 1G, 11 and 12 at 2.5G and the PoE module's ports - the vendor's platform data, read on the coprocessor.

rows.bay: faceplate, SFP cages on the switch
rows.note: Two 1G SFP cages on the switch chip (F1, F2). No transceiver data from the host: the cage EEPROMs are on the coprocessor's I2C.
The serial console at the back. There is no management port: the USB network adapter some benches add keeps its interface name.

port_types.comment: Drawing hints only. Width is in the same arbitrary units the renderer uses for a row; the shapes differ enough that a person recognises a copper socket from a cage at a glance.
